analysis.one_liner: Requires automakers to sell an ever-larger share of zero-emission cars until only zero-emission cars can be sold.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 8 Senate sponsors in May 2019, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to require vehicle manufacturers to sell a rising percentage of zero-emission passenger vehicles, starting at 50% by model year 2030 and reaching 100% by 2040. Manufacturers that fall short would have to buy zero-emission credits from manufacturers that exceed the target, with civil penalties for noncompliance deposited into the Highway Trust Fund. States could keep their own stricter rules, and after 2040 the EPA could block manufacture of any non-zero-emission passenger vehicle.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to vehicle pollution and to climate change, since the largest single source of US transportation emissions would be phased out on a fixed schedule. Drivers would also benefit over time because electric vehicles have lower fuel and maintenance costs. Buyers of electric vehicles and the manufacturers that build them gain, and a credit market would channel money to automakers that sell zero-emission vehicles early.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and communities exposed to vehicle pollution

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a firm, dated schedule — 50% zero-emission sales by 2030, rising 5 points a year to 100% by 2040 — after which manufacturers may sell only zero-emission passenger vehicles, giving automakers and consumers a predictable transition rather than voluntary targets.

A manufacturer that misses its required percentage must submit credits, and each zero-emission vehicle sold earns a credit that can be banked for up to five years or sold to a lagging manufacturer, so the standard is enforced through the market with civil penalties of twice the value of unmet credits deposited into the Highway Trust Fund.

The bill leaves state zero-emission vehicle rules in place, so states like California could keep stricter standards, and it preserves no special exemption for any manufacturer selling 100 or more vehicles a year.
After model year 2040, the EPA could seek an injunction to stop manufacture of any passenger vehicle other than a zero-emission vehicle, giving the standard permanent teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Vehicle manufacturers would bear compliance costs and, for laggards, credit purchases and civil penalties, costs likely to be passed partly to new-car buyers through higher prices during the transition. Petroleum refiners, fuel retailers, and parts suppliers tied to internal-combustion engines would lose sales as the fleet electrifies. The bill includes no direct funding for charging infrastructure or consumer purchase incentives, so households unable to afford a new electric vehicle in the early years would keep driving used gasoline cars while the standard binds only new sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Automakers, gasoline-related industries, early new-car buyers

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection is the pace: requiring 50% zero-emission sales by model year 2030 is far faster than the market or charging infrastructure was on track to deliver, which would raise new-car prices in the 2020s-2030s and could leave households that cannot afford a new electric car paying the transition's costs.

The bill relies entirely on supply-side mandates and a credit-trading market; it contains no purchase subsidies, charging-network funding, or used-vehicle provisions, so benefits would flow first to buyers of new vehicles while lower-income households feel mainly the price effects.

Credit trading lets a manufacturer keep selling gasoline vehicles by buying credits instead of selling zero-emission vehicles, which concentrates the compliance burden in credit prices and can route money from established automakers to early movers without cutting emissions beyond the schedule itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The environmental and health benefit of a dated, enforceable phase-out of new gasoline-car sales is large, and the design — a percentage schedule plus tradable credits plus penalties — is a proven mechanism states like California already use. The real cost falls unevenly: new-car buyers and the auto supply chain absorb the transition in its fast early years, and lower-income households, who buy used cars, get the air-quality benefits but not the cheaper-to-run electric vehicles at first. A slower ramp or paired consumer incentives would have eased those costs; as written, the bill asks a lot of the 2020s.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Zero-Emission Vehicles Act of 2019 on May 15, 2019, with Sens. Harris, Whitehouse, Sanders, Gillibrand, and Schatz as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced; that referral is the last entry in its action history.
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, no version passed either chamber, and the bill received no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers selling conventional gasoline vehicles, and petroleum and related fuel businesses, avoided a dated phase-out of their market; no member had to vote on the record for or against the standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gasoline-vehicle automakers and oil, unchallenged on the record

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as its sole sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Harris, Whitehouse, Sanders, Gillibrand, and Schatz
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill's cosponsor list totaled 7 (6 Democrats, 1 Independent).

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 15, 2019 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill died in committee without any recorded vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would force a rising share of their US sales to be zero-emission, reaching 100% by 2040, with credit purchases and civil penalties for shortfall. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the cleaner air and lower fuel costs the standard would deliver to the public.

A dated national standard would guarantee a growing market for their vehicles, and each zero-emission vehicle sold would earn a credit they could bank or sell to lagging competitors, creating a new revenue stream.

Phasing out new gasoline-vehicle sales would shrink future gasoline demand, the core of their consumer market. Their preference to keep the status quo conflicted with the bill's air-quality and climate goals for drivers and communities.
